leaves.title: Reading a short conversation for key information
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice a real reading strategy: getting the general idea of a conversation first, then going back to find specific details — rather than trying to understand every single word on the first read.

Read the conversation below once, quickly, just to get the general situation. Then read it again to answer the questions.

Jordan: Excuse me, is this seat free?
Priya: Yes, it is! Please, sit down.
Jordan: Thanks. Are you here on vacation?
Priya: No, we aren't. We're here for work. But today's a free day for us.
Jordan: Oh nice! Are you from around here?
Priya: No, we're from Chicago. We're here for a conference.
Jordan: Have a great day!
Priya: Thanks, you too!

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to read a short everyday conversation and pull out the key facts, even if you don't understand every word.
examples: Reading for gist means reading quickly for the general idea — who is speaking, and about what.
Reading for detail means going back to find a specific answer, like a name or a reason.
commonMistakes: Don't stop at every unknown word on the first read — keep going and get the general idea first.
Don't guess an answer without checking the text again — reading for detail means finding the exact information.

exercises.title: Answer the questions
exercises.instructions: Read the conversation again and write short answers.

questions.prompt: Is today a work day for Priya?

exercises.title: Choose the correct answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that matches the conversation.

leaves.title: Reading a short article with percentages
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice reading a short informational article that includes percentages — a common feature of everyday articles about surveys, studies, and habits.

Read the article below once for the general idea, then read it again to fill in the missing percentages and answer the questions.

Most People Have a Weekend Routine

A new survey asked two thousand people about their weekends. The results show that 72% of people do very similar things every Saturday and Sunday. Of these people, 58% say they usually relax and watch a show at home. 35% say they usually do housework, and only 15% say they usually try something new every weekend.

Researchers say a predictable weekend routine can help people feel less stressed after a busy work week. But a few people in the survey said they prefer a different plan every weekend, because routine feels boring to them.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to read a short survey-style article, understand percentages in context, and answer comprehension questions about it.
examples: '% = percent' — 72% means seventy-two out of every hundred people.
'Of these people' refers back to a group already mentioned, not everyone in the survey.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse the percentage of all survey respondents with the percentage of a smaller group mentioned afterward ('of these people') — read carefully to see which group a percentage refers to.
Don't skip the numbers when reading quickly — in a survey article, the percentages usually carry the most important information.

exercises.title: Answer the questions
exercises.instructions: Read the article again and answer each question.

questions.prompt: How many people were in the survey?
What percentage of people do similar things every weekend?
What percentage usually relax and watch a show at home?

exercises.title: Choose the correct answer
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that matches the article.
